newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan panel urges speedy decontrol of stock fees.
newsitem.headline: Japan panel urges speedy decontrol of stock fees.

text.p: Japan should move swiftly to liberalise commissions on stock transactions and should carry out the deregulation well before 2001, a key advisory panel proposed on Friday in an interim report.

"The liberalisation of commissions is a major pillar of the current reforms of the securities markets," said the report by the deregulation panel, which is advising the finance minister on securities issues.
"In order to improve efficiency, Japan needs to fully liberalise commissions on stock transactions of less than one billion yen as soon as possible, without waiting for 2001," it said.

This would mean that brokerages would be free to determine their own commission rates on securities trades below that value, which is expected to spur strong price competition and a possible shakeout in the domestic brokerage business.
However, the panel proposed a two-step process to avoid disrupting stock markets and avoid giving a sudden jolt to brokers' business.

It said that initially, from April 1998, the liberalisation should only cover stock transactions above a threshold set at less than 100 million yen, to smooth the transition to a deregulated environment. The second step would be to lift controls on trades below that level to achieve full liberalisation.
Japan liberalised commissions on big stock transactions above one billion yen in April 1994, but commissions on smaller-lot stock deals have remained at fixed levels.
The interim proposals were compiled by three working groups within the advisory panel, the Securities and Exchange Council.

The council is scheduled to finalise its proposals next month, to help Japan set a schedule for implementing its "Big Bang" reforms of financial markets. Financial sources say the final report will be automatically adopted by the ministry.

Last November, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled plans for a five-year Big Bang to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001 and catch up with reforms carried out years earlier in Europe and North America.

The panel also recommended in its interim report that Japan's tax authorities should think about abolishing securities transaction taxes in order to improve the efficiency of Japan's securities markets and to cut trading costs to internationally competitive levels.

In order to help brokers compete in deregulated markets and offer new financial products to Japanese investors, Japan should allow securities houses to start offering multi-service accounts and "wrap" accounts as a part of the "Big Bang" reforms, the panel said.

The multi-service accounts would allow customers to automatically transfer profits from stock sales to money management funds (MMFs), a type of investment trust investing mainly in medium-term government notes.
The panel also said Japan should consider measures to allow customers' credit card charges and public utility fees to be deducted from the accounts.

The wrap account system, widely used in the United States, allows a securities house to manage an investor's assets based on discretionary management contracts or by introducing third-party advisory firms to investors.
Such wrap accounts are banned under Japanese law.

Japan's Finance Ministry is expected to submit bills to revise the Securities and Exchange law to the next ordinary session of parliament starting in January 1998 in order to implement the "Big Bang" reforms, ministry officials said.
